hints: Look closely at the two structures and focus on what is different at the left-hand end of the molecule.
Notice that glucose has an aldehyde group, $\text{-CHO}$, while sorbitol has a primary alcohol group, $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$, in that same position.
Changing an aldehyde to an alcohol needs gain of hydrogen, so think about which of the four reagents acts as a reducing agent for carbonyls.
walkthrough:
**Spot what changes in the structures**

Look at the left end only. Everything else stays the same.

Glucose has $\text{H-C=O}$, an aldehyde. Sorbitol has $\text{HO-CH}_2-$, a primary alcohol.

**Identify the reaction type**

Aldehyde to primary alcohol is gain of hydrogen. That is reduction.

General change:
$$\text{R-CHO} + 2[H] \rightarrow \text{R-CH}_2\text{OH}$$

**Pick the reducing reagent**

Sodium borohydride, $\text{NaBH}_4$, is the classic mild reducing agent that reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols. It does not affect the alcohol groups already present, so glucose is cleanly converted to sorbitol.

options.A: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is a strong oxidising agent. It would oxidise the aldehyde in glucose further to a carboxylic acid, the opposite of what is needed here.
options.B: Sodium borohydride reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols by providing hydride. It converts the -CHO of glucose to -CH2OH to give sorbitol, leaving the other -OH groups unchanged.
options.C: Sodium hydroxide is a base, not a reducing agent. It cannot supply the hydrogen needed to reduce a carbonyl to an alcohol.
options.D: Tollens' reagent is a mild oxidising agent used to test for aldehydes. It oxidises aldehydes to carboxylates and gives a silver mirror, so it would oxidise glucose rather than reduce it to sorbitol.
